chapter_title: ROS Actions in C++ and Asynchronous Operation

screens.title: ROS Actions in C++ and Asynchronous Operation
screens.subtitle: Implement servers and clients, handle preemption, and monitor action topics across languages

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on writing ROS actions in C++ and running clients asynchronously so your robot can manage multiple tasks without blocking. You will learn the shape of a SimpleActionServer class, why boost::bind is required to register a class method as the execute callback, and how feedback, result, preemption, and cancellation are expressed in C++. We will also cover the client side: waitForServer, sendGoal with four callbacks, and how SimpleClientGoalState describes a completed goal. You will practice building the C++ node with the proper CMake add_dependencies step so generated action headers are available at compile time. Finally, we'll use rqt_graph to visualize the five topics an action creates and see how actionlib presents them as a single logical action. This matters because production robots favor C++ for lower latency and deterministic behavior, and asynchronous callbacks let one client monitor many actions at once. As we move through code examples and visualizations, keep an eye out for the common mistake of omitting add_dependencies and for confusing preemption with cancellation. By the end you will be able to implement, run, and diagnose a C++ action pair and reason about asynchronous interactions.

keyIdea.title: Big idea
keyIdea.text: C++ action servers give performance and control; asynchronous clients let a node manage multiple actions concurrently while rqt_graph reveals the underlying topics so you can debug communication.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of these screens you will implement a SimpleActionServer in C++ with callback-based goal handling, and implement a SimpleActionClient with asynchronous feedback and result callbacks. You will also correctly handle goal preemption and cancellation from within the server loop and use rqt_graph to confirm the action topics created by actionlib. Each objective is practical: writing the server teaches class structure, working with callbacks teaches safe multithreaded-style interactions, and using rqt_graph gives you a way to verify the runtime wiring of topics across nodes. For example, when you build the CountUntil server in C++, you will register executeCB with boost::bind and use a loop that publishes feedback at 2 hertz and checks isPreemptRequested; that pattern demonstrates how to end a goal cleanly or mark it preempted. A common misconception is that preemption is the same as cancellation; preemption is requested by the server or client to stop a running goal and must be explicitly acknowledged by setPreempted. Practically, mastering these objectives lets a robot run long-running actions reliably in production while monitoring progress and reacting to new commands.

screens.title: Why C++ for Action Servers
screens.subtitle: Performance, determinism, and memory control for production robots

narration.text: C++ is the favored language for action servers in production robotics because it gives lower latency and finer control over memory and C P U usage. In ROS, actions often power motion controllers or real-time monitoring where delays can cause poor behavior. A C++ implementation lets you place the feedback loop and cancellation checks within a tight, compiled loop, reducing overhead compared with interpreted code. For example, a CountUntil action that publishes frequent feedback at two hertz and checks preemption uses a ros::Rate sleep call and direct pointer access via a ConstPtr; this path avoids copying large payloads and keeps memory usage predictable. A common misconception is that Python cannot be used in production; Python is fine for prototyping and many nodes, but when timing or resource budgets are strict, C++ is preferred. Practically, you should choose C++ for servers that run in the control or sensor processing path. To cement this idea, implement a simple server that counts to ten and measure response to a cancel request; you will see the C++ server accept preemption and respond immediately. What property of your robot's workload would push you to choose C++ over Python?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: C++ action servers offer predictable timing and minimal runtime overhead—use them when latency or memory determinism matters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Why C++ for Action Servers
Definition

C++ provides compiled performance and tighter control over resources, which matters for servers that must reply to preemption and publish frequent feedback without delay.

When to prefer C++
Control loops, motion control, sensor fusion, or any task where timing is critical.
Common misconception
Choosing C++ is required for all nodes — false. Use C++ for performance-sensitive servers, Python for rapid prototyping.
Key Takeaway

Use C++ when you need reliable timing, low latency, and tight memory behavior for action servers.

Concrete example: CountUntil server
A server loops from 1 to max_number at 2 hertz, publishes feedback percentage, checks isPreemptRequested each iteration, and calls setSucceeded on success. The C++ path uses a CountUntilGoalConstPtr to avoid copying the request.
<!-- snippet adapted from chapter -->
void executeCB(const my_first_robot::CountUntilGoalConstPtr& goal) {
  ros::Rate rate(2);
  for (int i=1; i<=goal->max_number; ++i) {
    if (_as.isPreemptRequested()) {
      _as.setPreempted();
      return;
    }
    my_first_robot::CountUntilFeedback feedback;
    feedback.percentage = float(i) / float(goal->max_number);
    _as.publishFeedback(feedback);
    rate.sleep();
  }
  my_first_robot::CountUntilResult result;
  result.count = goal->max_number;
  _as.setSucceeded(result);
}
Analogy
C++ action servers are like a compiled controller board: minimal overhead and tight timing.
Check your understanding
Why is ConstPtr used for the goal? Hint: think about copying versus referencing.

screens.title: Implementing SimpleActionServer in C++
screens.subtitle: Class layout, constructor binding, and starting the server

narration.text: Let's walk through the structure of a SimpleActionServer implemented in C++. The server is typically a class that holds a member of type actionlib::SimpleActionServer<YourAction>. That member is constructed with the node handle, the action name, and a bound execute callback. Because executeCB is a class method, you wrap it with boost::bind and pass this as the target object; the _1 placeholder represents the goal pointer the server will supply. Starting the server in the constructor with _as. start() registers it with ROS so it will accept goals. The executeCB receives a CountUntilGoalConstPtr, which is a constant shared pointer. Using ConstPtr avoids unnecessary copying of goal data and reduces latency. The executeCB pattern in the CountUntil example shows a loop that publishes feedback and checks _as. isPreemptRequested. If preemption is requested, call _as. setPreempted and exit. On success, prepare a result message and call _as. setSucceeded. A common mistake is forgetting to call start() or binding the wrong method signature; both prevent the server from receiving goals. Now inspect the core constructor snippet and mapping between class members, binding, and start.

keyIdea.title: Server anatomy
keyIdea.text: A server class owns SimpleActionServer, binds executeCB with boost::bind, starts the server, and publishes feedback and results while honoring preemption.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › SimpleActionServer Walkthrough
Constructor & binding
// in CountUntilServer constructor
_as(nh, "/count_until", boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1), false) {
  _as.start();
  ROS_INFO("CountUntil server is ready.");
}

void executeCB(const my_first_robot::CountUntilGoalConstPtr& goal) {
  // process loop publishes feedback, checks preemption, then setSucceeded
}
Note how boost::bind wraps the member function and this pointer so the server can call executeCB with the goal argument. Omitting the final false or failing to call start would alter server behavior.
Why ConstPtr
ConstPtr avoids copying goal data and expresses immutability of the received request.
Misstep
Binding a free function instead of a member will not give access to class state; ensure you bind this.
Process: goal lifecycle
  1. Server constructed with name and a bound execute callback.
  2. Server start() enables goal acceptance.
  3. executeCB receives a ConstPtr goal and performs the work loop.
  4. Publish feedback regularly; check isPreemptRequested to respect cancellation.
  5. Call setSucceeded or setPreempted based on outcome.
Key Takeaway

Bind executeCB with boost::bind, start the server, and ensure the execute loop both publishes feedback and honors preemption.

screens.title: Handling Preemption and Cancellation
screens.subtitle: Detecting requests and stopping work cleanly in the execute loop

narration.text: Handling preemption and cancellation is essential to keep a server responsive when new commands arrive. In C++ action servers the common pattern is to check _as. isPreemptRequested inside the executeCB loop. If a client or another part of the system requests preemption or cancellation, isPreemptRequested returns true and you should call _as. setPreempted to indicate the goal did not complete normally. This differentiates from simply stopping work: setPreempted informs clients and higher-level logic that the goal was intentionally interrupted. The CountUntil server demonstrates this: the loop iterates from one to max_number, publishes feedback each step, and checks for preemption every iteration. If preempted, it logs, calls setPreempted, and breaks out. A common confusion is treating cancelGoal on the client as identical to server-side preemption; cancelGoal requests cancellation, but the server must inspect and acknowledge it. Practical exercise: send a goal to count to ten, sleep three seconds, then cancel; observe how the server sets the goal preempted and the client done callback reports the final state. Why is explicit setPreempted important for system-level correctness? Handling Preemption and Cancellation means check ispreemptrequested regularly and call setpreempted to acknowledge cancellation and let clients observe the interrupted state.. In practical terms, detecting requests and stopping work cleanly in the execute loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Preemption flow
keyIdea.text: Check isPreemptRequested regularly and call setPreempted to acknowledge cancellation and let clients observe the interrupted state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Preemption & Cancellation
Step-by-step: server check loop
1. Begin executeCB and read goal parameters from ConstPtr.
2. Start a loop to perform work, e.g., counting with ros::Rate sleep.
3. At each iteration call _as.isPreemptRequested().
4. If true, call _as.setPreempted() and exit the loop.
5. If loop completes, fill a result and call _as.setSucceeded(result).
Example scenario
Client sends goal to count to 10. After 3 seconds the client calls cancelGoal. The server sees isPreemptRequested on the next iteration, calls setPreempted, and the client receives a done callback reporting a preempted state.
Common mistakes
  • Not checking isPreemptRequested often enough — delays responding to cancel requests.
  • Calling setSucceeded without verifying the goal completed — hides cancellations from clients.
  • Assuming cancel always immediately stops work — server must cooperate by checking and acknowledging.
Pro tip

Check preemption at predictable points in your loop and make the acknowledgement explicit with setPreempted for clearer debugging.

screens.title: SimpleActionClient in C++
screens.subtitle: sendGoal with callbacks: active, feedback, and done

narration.text: On the client side, the C++ SimpleActionClient pattern gives you non-blocking interactions through callbacks. After constructing the client and waiting for the server with waitForServer, you create a goal and call sendGoal. The sendGoal method accepts up to three callback bindings: a done callback invoked when the action finishes, an active callback when the goal becomes active, and a feedback callback invoked repeatedly with progress updates. In the CountUntil example, feedbackCB receives a CountUntilFeedbackConstPtr and logs the percentage, activeCB logs that the goal is active, and doneCB receives a SimpleClientGoalState and a CountUntilResultConstPtr so you can inspect the final state and result. You can also cancel goals via _ac. cancelGoal() from the client. A practical misconception is expecting sendGoal to block until completion; it does not. This asynchronous behavior lets your node monitor multiple actions simultaneously. As a concrete exercise, create a client that sends a goal of 10, sleeps three seconds, then cancels — observe the feedback callback and final doneCB state to verify proper cancellation handling. SimpleActionClient in C++ means sendgoal registers done/active/feedback callbacks and returns immediately so the node can remain responsive and manage many actions.. In practical terms, sendgoal with callbacks: active, feedback, and done. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client callbacks
keyIdea.text: sendGoal registers done/active/feedback callbacks and returns immediately so the node can remain responsive and manage many actions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › SimpleActionClient
Client core snippet
// create client and send goal
CountUntilClient() : _ac("/count_until", true) {
  _ac.waitForServer();
}

void sendGoal(int max_number) {
  my_first_robot::CountUntilGoal goal;
  goal.max_number = max_number;
  _ac.sendGoal(goal,
               boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::doneCB, this, _1, _2),
               boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::activeCB, this),
               boost::bind(&CountUntilClient::feedbackCB, this, _1));
}
Note the three bindings: done, active, and feedback. The client remains responsive after sendGoal, and you may call cancelGoal to request termination.
Callbacks explained
  • activeCB: notifies when the goal becomes active on the server side.
  • feedbackCB: receives ongoing feedback messages such as percentage complete.
  • doneCB: called when the action completes; receives a SimpleClientGoalState and a result pointer.
Example
Send a goal of 10, sleep three seconds, then call cancelGoal. The feedbackCB will run several times and the doneCB will report a cancelled or preempted final state.
Common misconception

sendGoal blocks until the action completes — false. It returns immediately and uses callbacks to notify progress and completion.

screens.title: boost::bind, member callbacks, and ConstPtr semantics
screens.subtitle: How C++ binds class methods as callbacks and why goal pointers are ConstPtr

narration.text: Two small but essential C++ idioms appear repeatedly in action code: boost::bind for binding class member functions and the use of ConstPtr for received message pointers. C++ member functions require an implicit this pointer, so you cannot pass &Class::method directly to an A P I expecting a free function. boost::bind resolves this by wrapping the member method and providing this along with placeholders such as _1 for the incoming goal pointer. In the CountUntilServer constructor you will see boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1). This yields a callable that the action server can invoke with the goal pointer. The goal type is provided as a ConstPtr — a constant shared pointer — because the server should treat the incoming goal as read-only and avoid extra copies. This reduces memory churn and improves performance when large goals or many requests are present. A common mistake is binding a callback with the wrong signature or forgetting placeholders; this prevents the server from receiving the correct arguments at runtime. Try editing the signature and observe the compile-time errors or misbehavior; binding correctly is a small syntactic task with big runtime consequences.

keyIdea.title: Binding & pointers
keyIdea.text: boost::bind wraps member methods so the action server can call them; ConstPtr ensures efficient, read-only access to goal data.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › boost::bind & ConstPtr
Visual mapping: bind wraps method + this
Binding pattern
boost::bind(&CountUntilServer::executeCB, this, _1) — _1 is the goal pointer placeholder the action server will pass.
ConstPtr meaning
The goal arrives as CountUntilGoalConstPtr. Treat it as read-only and avoid copying to keep performance predictable.
If you bind without the placeholder or with the wrong signature, the code will either fail to compile or the server will call the wrong function prototype. Fix binding issues by matching signatures and including placeholders for each parameter the action server supplies.
Example consequences
When callbacks are bound correctly, the server receives goals and can publish feedback. When binding is wrong, the server may not start or might throw runtime errors. ConstPtr reduces copying; if you need a mutable copy for long-lived work, explicitly copy into a local message and manage lifetime.
Check your understanding
Why prefer ConstPtr over passing by value for large messages? Consider memory allocation and copy semantics.
Key Takeaway

Use boost::bind with correct placeholders to expose member functions as callbacks, and use ConstPtr to avoid copies and signify immutability.

screens.title: CMakeLists and add_dependencies
screens.subtitle: Why action headers must be generated before compilation

narration.text: A frequent build-time failure when writing C++ nodes that depend on custom actions is compiling before the action message headers exist. Catkin generates action headers from your action definition files during the build; to ensure the C++ target runs after that generation, you must add add_dependencies in CMakeLists. txt pointing to the exported targets of the action package. The example shows add_dependencies(count_until_server ${my_first_robot_EXPORTED_TARGETS}). This ensures the count_until_server target waits until my_first_robot's action headers are generated. Without this, the compiler will not find CountUntilAction. h and the build fails. Another related item is target_link_libraries with ${catkin_LIBRARIES} to link ROS client libraries. Practically, when you add a new action or message, update package. xml and CMakeLists accordingly and rebuild with catkin_make or catkin build. A quick test is to remove add_dependencies intentionally and observe a missing header error; then restore the dependency and confirm the build succeeds. This small build rule prevents a common, frustrating error and speeds development. CMakeLists and add_dependencies means add_dependencies ensures generated action headers exist before the c++ target is compiled, avoiding missing-header build errors.. In practical terms, why action headers must be generated before compilation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CMake rule
keyIdea.text: add_dependencies ensures generated action headers exist before the C++ target is compiled, avoiding missing-header build errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › CMake & add_dependencies
CMake excerpt
find_package(catkin REQUIRED COMPONENTS
  roscpp
  actionlib
  actionlib_msgs
  my_first_robot
)

add_executable(count_until_server src/count_until_server.cpp)
add_dependencies(count_until_server ${my_first_robot_EXPORTED_TARGETS})
target_link_libraries(count_until_server ${catkin_LIBRARIES})
The add_dependencies line serializes the build so that my_first_robot's exported targets, which include generated headers, finish before compiling the server target.
Why this matters
Action headers are generated from .action files during build. If your C++ node is compiled too early, the compiler cannot find the generated header, causing cryptic errors. add_dependencies is the standard catkin solution to order generation before compilation.
Lab check
Remove add_dependencies and run the build to see the error, then re-add it and confirm the fix. This demonstrates how build ordering affects generated artifacts.
Key Takeaway

Always add build dependencies for targets that rely on generated messages or actions so compilation order is correct.

screens.title: Cross-language action interoperability
screens.subtitle: How Python clients and C++ servers communicate using the same action protocol

narration.text: One of ROS's strengths is language-agnostic messaging. A C++ action server and a Python client speak the same action protocol by using shared message definitions. The CountUntil example is a perfect demonstration: the action definition describes goal, feedback, and result messages; Catkin generates headers for C++ and Python message bindings. When you run a Python client against a C++ server, actionlib translates the calls into the five underlying topics—goal, cancel, feedback, result, and status—so both sides interoperate. In rqt_graph you can toggle the Actions checkbox to show a single block or inspect the five topics individually. A practical exercise is to run the C++ server and the Python client from Chapter 4.1 and verify that feedback and results arrive correctly. A common misconception is that different languages require special adapters; in ROS the messages and actionlib handle translation so you can mix languages seamlessly. Reflect: after testing cross-language communication, consider what kinds of errors would come from mismatched message definitions or forgetting to rebuild generated headers. Cross-language action interoperability means actions are language-agnostic: shared action definitions and generated bindings let python clients talk to c++ servers over the same underlying topics.. In practical terms, how python clients and c++ servers communicate using the same action protocol. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cross-language
keyIdea.text: Actions are language-agnostic: shared action definitions and generated bindings let Python clients talk to C++ servers over the same underlying topics.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › Cross-language Interop
Comparison: Python client vs C++ server
Common ground
Both sides use the same action definition; actionlib maps protocol messages to the five topics so they can interoperate.
Differences
C++ favors ConstPtr and boost::bind; Python uses direct functions and simpler callback registration. The runtime protocol is identical.
Exercise
Run count_until_server (C++) and the Python client from Chapter 4.1. Observe feedback messages and final result. Then reverse roles: run Python server and C++ client. Confirm both combinations work and inspect rqt_graph.
Key Takeaway

Message definitions, not language, define compatibility. Keep action definitions consistent and rebuild generated code after changes.

screens.title: rqt_graph and the five action topics
screens.subtitle: Seeing goal, cancel, feedback, result, and status as topic connections

narration.text: rqt_graph is the practical tool to inspect how actionlib translates an action into underlying topics. When a server and client are running, actionlib creates five topics for each action name: goal, cancel, feedback, result, and status. If you leave the Actions checkbox enabled in rqt_graph, the action appears as a single logical block. If you uncheck Actions, those five topics are shown individually and you can trace publishers and subscribers. This helps you debug mismatches and confirm cross-language traffic. For example, run a C++ CountUntil server and a Python client, open rqt_graph, and look for /count_until/goal and /count_until/feedback to verify which node publishes and which subscribes. A common troubleshooting step is to toggle the Actions view to expose the topics and ensure the expected publishers and subscribers exist. In multi-action systems, use rqt_graph to confirm that feedback topics are coming from the right server and that status messages are visible so you know the action state transitions are happening as expected. What would you look for if feedback stops arriving? rqt_graph and the five action topics means toggle actions to see either a single action block or the five explicit topics for deeper debugging of action communications.. In practical terms, seeing goal, cancel, feedback, result, and status as topic connections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: rqt_graph tip
keyIdea.text: Toggle Actions to see either a single action block or the five explicit topics for deeper debugging of action communications.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › rqt_graph & Action Topics
Action topics to check
  • /count_until/goal — publishes new goals.
  • /count_until/cancel — client cancels are published here.
  • /count_until/feedback — server sends progress updates.
  • /count_until/result — final result message is published by server.
  • /count_until/status — actionlib status messages about goal states.
Debug workflow
Run server and client, open rqt_graph, uncheck Actions to reveal the individual topics, and confirm which node is publishing each topic to diagnose missing messages.
Example check
If feedback stops arriving, inspect /count_until/feedback publisher. If the server publishes but the client does not receive it, check topic namespace mismatches and verify both nodes use the same action name.
Pro tip

Toggle Actions in rqt_graph to switch between high-level and topic-level views; this quickly narrows down communication issues.

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points you should carry forward. First, implement performance-sensitive action servers in C++ using a class that owns a SimpleActionServer, bind executeCB with boost::bind, and start the server in the constructor. Second, the C++ SimpleActionClient is asynchronous: use waitForServer, sendGoal with done, active, and feedback callbacks, and cancelGoal to request termination. Third, always add add_dependencies in CMakeLists. txt for targets depending on generated action headers so builds do not fail. These three ideas — server structure, client callbacks, and build dependencies — form the practical core that makes C++ actions reliable and maintainable. As you practice, verify communication using rqt_graph and test cross-language scenarios to ensure your action definition is consistent. Which of these three would you check first if a goal never becomes active? screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you code

narration.text: Before you start coding, hold three brief reminders in mind. First, when you register a class method as a callback use boost::bind with this and the correct placeholders so the server can call your executeCB properly. Second, always check for preemption inside executeCB loops and call setPreempted to acknowledge cancellation so clients see the interrupted state. Third, configure your CMakeLists with add_dependencies for packages that export generated action headers to avoid build-time missing-header errors. These three checks will prevent the most common runtime and build errors as you implement the CountUntil server and client. After implementing and testing, use rqt_graph to confirm topics and try cross-language communication to validate the action protocol works across both Python and C++. Module 5 › Chapter 4.2 › What to Remember
Bind correctly
Use boost::bind(&Class::method, this, _1) for member callbacks.
Handle preemption
Check isPreemptRequested and call setPreempted to acknowledge cancellation.
Build rules
add_dependencies ensures action headers are generated before compiling your node.
Next steps

Implement the CountUntil C++ server and client, verify with rqt_graph, and then test cross-language interactions. Keep this checklist handy while you code.
